notes.b: No country makes or grows everything it needs, so countries depend on one another. The key idea is the effects that follow when a decision is taken in one place and the results land in another.
points: Countries and regions rely on each other for raw materials, components (parts used to make a product), markets (places to sell), investment, labour, food and a shared environment, so a decision in one place has effects elsewhere.
Globalisation (the growing links between countries), through trade, multinational companies (firms operating in many countries), communications and migration, has deepened this interdependence.
It has an economic form (trading patterns), an environmental form (shared global issues) and a political and social form (decisions on refugees, migration and human rights).
notes.tip: Write every issue as interdependence: name the decision or action, where it was taken, and where the effects fall. An essay that only describes deforestation or refugees without that link scores poorly.

notes.b: A global product is made in some places and bought in others. Geographers call these producer regions and consumer regions, and the gap between them explains who gains most from trade.
points: Producer regions supply raw materials, components and assembly (putting the parts together). These are often developing countries with low wages, which is why firms locate this work there.
Consumer regions buy the finished product. These are mostly rich countries, and increasingly China and India, because their people have the income to buy it.

Value added (the extra worth created at each stage of making and selling a product) is shared very unequally along the chain: most of it is captured by design, branding and retail in consumer regions.
notes.tip: For an 80-mark essay on one company, cover the company and its product, producer regions with named places and positive and negative impacts, consumer regions, Ireland's role, the uneven share of value, and an evaluation.

notes.b: Apple is the main case study of a multinational whose product is designed in one country, built from parts made in several others, and sold worldwide. Following the iPhone shows how many regions one product links.
points: Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, with headquarters in Cupertino, California (Apple Park, 2017). The iPhone launched in 2007.
Apple designs in California, where its headquarters are. Its packaging states: 'Designed by Apple in California. Assembled in China.'
TSMC in Taiwan makes Apple's A-series and M-series chips (the processors inside its devices). Samsung and LG in South Korea supply screens, so no single country makes the whole phone.
Other components come from further suppliers around the world. Minerals include cobalt (a metal used in batteries), most of which is mined in the DR Congo.
Foxconn (Hon Hai Precision Industry), a Taiwanese contract manufacturer (a firm that builds products for other companies), assembles most iPhones in China, at Zhengzhou and Shenzhen.
Foxconn and the Indian Tata group assemble iPhones in India near Chennai and Bengaluru, so assembly is spreading beyond China.
Apple's largest sales regions are the Americas, Europe and Greater China, so its customers are spread across three continents.
notes.tip: Foxconn is Taiwanese, with its main plants in mainland China. Apple's Cork campus does not make iPhones.

notes.b: For the regions that make and supply the parts, Apple's orders bring real benefits but also costs. A good answer gives both sides, with named places.
points: Positive: assembly and supply firms provide jobs for millions of people, bringing skills, industrial growth and export earnings to China.
Positive: supplier firms grow because of Apple's orders, as TSMC and Foxconn show.

Negative: a 2011 study by Kenneth Kraemer, Greg Linden and Jason Dedrick estimated that Apple kept about 58% of the sale price of an iPhone (2010 model) as profit, while Chinese assembly labour received under 2%. This shows how unequally value is shared.

Negative: a cluster of worker suicides at Foxconn's Shenzhen factories in 2010 drew attention to long hours, strict discipline and pressure. Foxconn raised wages and put up safety nets (nets fixed to buildings to stop people falling), a response to the attention.
Negative: in November 2022 workers at Foxconn's Zhengzhou plant protested over pay and COVID-19 lockdown conditions, delaying iPhone supplies worldwide.
Negative: producer regions depend on Apple's orders, which can move. Some assembly has shifted to India, which shows that the orders can move.
Negative: Amnesty International (2016) documented child labour in the DR Congo's hand-dug cobalt mines, which supply the metal for batteries.
notes.tip: Do not give a Foxconn wage, Apple's revenue or profits, or child-labour figures beyond those given here. Examiners expect the uneven share of value to be part of the evaluation.

notes.b: Rich consumer regions gain the product and keep the most valuable parts of the chain, but they also send problems back to poorer countries.
points: Consumers in rich countries gain access to new technology and services, paying high prices for products whose assembly is cheap.
Most profit and the high-paid design and marketing jobs stay in the USA, because the company is based there.
Electronic waste from discarded devices is exported to poorer countries.

notes.b: Ireland is both a place where Apple employs people and a country affected by decisions taken elsewhere about Apple. This is a good example of how one firm links a small economy to the EU and the USA.
points: Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980, its first manufacturing plant in Europe. It now has about 6,000 employees in Cork and its European headquarters there.
Apple's Cork campus does not assemble iPhones. Its role is European headquarters and support, not the Chinese assembly chain.

In 2016 the European Commission ruled that Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth €13 billion. This was the recovery of illegal State aid (help from a government that breaks EU competition rules), not a fine, and Ireland argued against collecting it.
The General Court overturned the decision in 2020. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice reinstated it, and Ireland received about €14 billion, including interest.
A decision in Brussels therefore affected both Ireland and the USA, where the company is based.
US tariffs (taxes on imports) on many Chinese goods from 2018, and higher tariffs on most countries' imports in 2025, have pushed Apple to move some assembly to India.
notes.tip: The Apple tax case was the recovery of illegal State aid, not a fine, and Ireland argued against collecting it. Do not say Cork makes iPhones.

notes.h: Cadbury and Mondelēz: the company and its Irish plants
notes.b: Cadbury shows how a long-established British brand became part of an American multinational, and how Irish plants fit into its chain. It is a food company, so its chain begins on farms.
points: Cadbury was founded by John Cadbury in Birmingham, England, in 1824, so its origins are British. Its Bournville factory and model village for workers opened in 1879.
The American firm Kraft Foods took over Cadbury in 2010. In 2012 Kraft's snacks business, including Cadbury, became Mondelēz International, headquartered in Chicago.
Because Mondelēz is American, Cadbury is no longer a British-owned company.
Cadbury Ireland has a chocolate factory at Coolock, Dublin, and a chocolate crumb plant at Rathmore, Co. Kerry.
Rathmore uses milk from local dairy farms to make chocolate crumb (milk, sugar and cocoa), which is sent to Cadbury factories in Britain. It makes crumb, not finished bars.
notes.tip: Rathmore makes chocolate crumb, not finished bars. Do not say Cadbury still belongs to a British company: Mondelēz is American.

notes.h: Cadbury and Mondelēz: cocoa producer regions
notes.b: The cocoa in chocolate comes mainly from West Africa, where small farmers earn little and face serious problems. These points cover who grows cocoa, how their incomes are supported, and the child labour in the trade.
points: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, with about two-fifths of world output. Ghana is second. Together they grow over half of the world's cocoa, mostly exported as beans, so these two countries depend on one crop.
Most cocoa is grown on small family farms of a few hectares, so individual farmers have little power over the price they are paid.
From the 2020–21 season Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana added, because farm incomes were low, a Living Income Differential of 400 US dollars a tonne to cocoa sales to raise farmers' incomes.

A study for the US Department of Labor by NORC at the University of Chicago, published in 2020, found about 1.56 million children in child labour in cocoa growing in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana (2018–19).
The Harkin–Engel Protocol (2001) committed the chocolate industry to end the worst forms of child labour in cocoa. Deadlines have been missed repeatedly.
Irish dairy farms supplying Rathmore are also a producer region for the company.
notes.tip: Do not give a cocoa farmer's share of the chocolate price or child-labour figures other than the NORC 1.56 million.

notes.h: Cadbury and Mondelēz: forests, price swings and value added
notes.b: Cocoa growing also changes the land, and a country that depends on one export is exposed to price swings. Most of the profit from processing is made far from the farms.
points: Côte d'Ivoire has lost most of its forest since independence (1960), much of it to cocoa farms, because farmers clear forest to plant more cocoa.
In 2024 cocoa prices rose to a record above 10,000 US dollars a tonne after poor West African harvests, caused by bad weather and the cocoa swollen shoot virus.
Farmers gained far less than the world price, because their governments fix farm-gate prices (the price paid to the farmer) in advance.
Value is mostly added outside Africa. The Netherlands, through the port of Amsterdam, is the world's largest cocoa-processing centre (where beans are turned into cocoa products).

notes.b: The company has made several choices about how it buys cocoa. One of them has been disputed.
points: Cadbury Dairy Milk carried the Fairtrade Mark (a label guaranteeing farmers a fairer deal) from 2009.
Mondelēz launched its own sustainability programme, Cocoa Life, in 2012, to improve cocoa farming, with about 400 million US dollars committed over ten years.
In 2017 Cadbury Dairy Milk in Britain and Ireland replaced the Fairtrade Mark with the Cocoa Life logo. Fair-trade campaigners criticised the decision.

notes.b: Chocolate is bought mostly by richer countries, which also keep most of its price. Their shoppers and governments can in turn pressure the producers.
points: Europe and North America consume most of the world's chocolate. Brands, marketing and retail take most of the price, because they add the most value.
Consumer campaigns and EU rules pass pressure back to producers, so a decision in a consumer region changes how farms are run.

The EU Deforestation Regulation (adopted 2023) will require firms selling cocoa, coffee, beef, soya, palm oil, rubber and timber in the EU to prove the goods were not grown on land deforested after 2020. Its application has been delayed.
notes.tip: Link the consumer side back to producers: brands and retail take most of the price, while consumer pressure and EU rules push producers to change.

notes.b: Intel is a shorter alternative case study of a multinational, useful if you studied it in the economic option. Its chain runs from design in the USA to factories and customers around the world.
points: Intel was founded in 1968 in Mountain View, California, and is headquartered in Santa Clara. Research and design are based in Oregon and California.

Wafers (thin discs of silicon from which chips are cut) are made in fabs (chip factories) at Hillsboro (Oregon), Chandler (Arizona), Leixlip and Kiryat Gat (Israel). Leixlip makes processor wafers, not computers.
Assembly and test (the final stages, away from the wafer fabs) take place in Penang and Kulim (Malaysia), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) and Chengdu (China).
Customers are computer makers, such as Lenovo, HP and Dell, which sell worldwide.
Intel's Leixlip fab has operated since 1989, and over €30 billion had been invested by 2023. Fab 34 opened in 2023.
49% of the Fab 34 joint venture (a business shared between two firms) was sold to Apollo Global Management for about $11 billion (2024).

Decisions elsewhere affect Intel: the US CHIPS and Science Act 2022 (about $50 billion, US support for chip making), about 15,000 global job cuts announced in August 2024, and a US government stake of about 10% (2025).
notes.tip: Intel Leixlip makes processor wafers, not computers.

notes.h: Irish trade and multinationals in Ireland
notes.b: Ireland is a small, open economy that acts as a producer region for American multinationals. This makes it successful in trade but exposed to decisions taken in Washington, Brussels and London.
points: Goods exports passed €200 billion in 2024 (CSO), and about a third went to the USA. Pharmaceutical and chemical products are the largest category.
Ireland has a large goods trade surplus (exports worth more than imports), the largest of it with the USA, because so much is exported there.

Ireland is a producer region for US multinationals: Pfizer at Ringaskiddy, Co. Cork, in pharmaceuticals; a medical-devices cluster in Galway, including Medtronic and Boston Scientific; and computer services, where Ireland is one of the world's largest exporters.
IDA Ireland, set up in 1949 to attract foreign firms, has client firms employing about 300,000 people (2023–24).
Dependence on US firms and markets makes Ireland vulnerable to US tax and tariff decisions. In early 2025 Irish exports to the USA rose sharply as US buyers stockpiled medicines before new tariffs.
Brexit, a political decision, changed Irish trade routes and agri-food exports. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, and the transition ended on 31 December 2020.
Corporation tax (the tax on company profits) is 12.5%, rising to 15% for very large groups from 2024 under the OECD agreement.
notes.tip: Ireland's role is a producer region for US firms, and the point to make is its vulnerability to US tax and tariff decisions.

notes.b: Deforestation means clearing forest permanently, usually for farming or mining. It is a global issue because the land is cleared where trees grow but the demand comes from other regions.
points: Forests cover about 31% of the world's land, so clearing them changes the planet at scale, about 4.06 billion hectares (FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020).
About 10 million hectares a year were deforested in 2015–2020, so the loss continues every year.
Most loss is in the tropics (the warm regions near the equator), in regions such as South America, Africa and South-East Asia.
Loss is driven largely by demand in other regions for beef, soya, palm oil, timber, cocoa and minerals, so consumers far away help cause clearance.
notes.tip: For each issue give the causes with the distant demand or decision, the effects locally and elsewhere, responses needing co-operation, and named examples.

notes.b: The Amazon shows how demand for food and animal feed in Europe and China helps drive clearance in Brazil.
points: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, with about 60% of it in Brazil.
Close to a fifth of the original forest has been cleared. Cattle ranching is the largest cause, because forest is cut down to make pasture.
Soya, much of it exported as animal feed to Europe and China, has spread north from Mato Grosso. Brazil is the world's largest exporter of soya beans.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway was begun in the early 1970s, and roads, mining and dams add to clearance, because roads open forest to settlers and farmers.

PRODES (Brazil's satellite monitoring of clearance) recorded annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon of about 27,800 km² in 2004, about 4,600 km² in 2012 and about 13,000 km² in 2021, with a sharp fall from 2023.
notes.tip: Do not say the Amazon produces 20% of the world's oxygen. This is a widely repeated error.

notes.h: Deforestation: the Amazon, effects and responses
notes.b: Clearing the Amazon harms people and climates far from Brazil, and the responses involve other countries too.
points: Effects elsewhere: the carbon released adds to global warming, reduced rainfall recycling (the forest returning moisture to the air) affects farming beyond the forest, biodiversity is lost, and indigenous peoples are threatened.
Scientists warn that the loss of about 20–25% of the forest could push parts of it towards degraded savanna (open grassland with few trees).
Brazil's Forest Code requires 80% of Amazon land to be kept as a legal reserve, so only 20% of a holding may be cleared.
Chico Mendes, a campaigner for the forest, was murdered on 22 December 1988.

Responses involving other countries: the Amazon Soy Moratorium (2006), agreed by traders; the Amazon Fund (2008), with Norway as the largest donor; and the EU Deforestation Regulation, which sets rules on goods sold in the EU.

notes.b: In South-East Asia the driver is palm oil, an ingredient in many everyday goods. Clearance in one country has even affected its neighbours.
points: Indonesia and Malaysia produce about 85% of the world's palm oil, used in foods, cosmetics and biofuels sold worldwide.
Peat swamp forest (waterlogged forest on thick layers of partly rotted plant matter) in Borneo and Sumatra is cleared and burned to plant oil palms.
Regional haze (smoke pollution) in 1997 and 2015 affected Singapore and Malaysia, a transboundary effect (one that crosses a border) of clearance in another country.
The Bornean orangutan is listed as Critically Endangered (IUCN, 2016), because its forest home is being lost.

notes.h: Managed forests in Scandinavia: Sweden and Finland
notes.b: Not all forest use is destructive. Sweden and Finland, Europe's most forested countries, use forests for a major export industry while keeping the stock of trees growing.
points: About two-thirds of Sweden's land is forest. About three-quarters of Finland's land is forest, the highest share in the EU.
Sweden's first Forestry Act (1903) required forest owners to replant after felling. The Forestry Act of 1993 gave equal weight to timber production and environmental goals.

Sweden's standing timber volume has roughly doubled since its National Forest Inventory began in the 1920s, because growth exceeds felling. This is sustainable yield (cutting no more than grows back).

Sweden and Finland are among the world's leading exporters of pulp, paper and sawn timber. IKEA, a Swedish company, is a major buyer of wood, so foreign demand supports the industry. UPM and Stora Enso are Finnish–Swedish forest companies.
notes.tip: Present the Scandinavian case as interdependence: buyers in other countries demand certified wood, which shapes how forests are run.

notes.h: Managed forests in Scandinavia: certification and criticism
notes.b: Buyers abroad can pressure producers to manage forests well, but the methods used are still criticised.
points: Buyers in other countries demand certification (independent proof that wood comes from well-managed forests): the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), founded in 1993, and PEFC (Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification), from 1999.
Clear-felling (cutting all trees in an area at once) followed by replanting, mostly with Norway spruce and Scots pine, is the main method.
Critics say clear-felling creates even-aged monocultures (stands of one kind of tree, all the same age), removes old-growth forest and dead wood, and threatens forest species.

Clear-felling destroys the lichen that reindeer graze on in winter, causing conflict with Sámi reindeer herders in northern Sweden. Their grievance is about grazing and land use, not forestry as a whole.
The Scandinavian case shows, in short, that that a forest economy can be managed sustainably when the state, owners and consumers act together.
notes.tip: Sámi grievances are about reindeer grazing and land use. Do not describe the Sámi as opposing all forestry.

notes.b: Ireland has little forest, so it relies on imports, which links Irish consumers to forest loss elsewhere.
points: Ireland's forest cover is about 11%, mostly conifer plantations. Sitka spruce, from western North America, is the main tree.
Coillte, the State forestry company, was set up in 1988. Private owners also hold forest.
About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900, so today's cover is a large rise from a very low base.
Ireland imports products linked to tropical deforestation, such as palm oil and feed for beef, so Irish consumers are part of the chain.

notes.b: Desertification is a common exam topic, and it is easy to define it wrongly. It is about damage to the land, not about sand spreading.
points: Desertification is land degradation (loss of the land's ability to support plants and crops) in drylands (areas with little rain). It is not the desert advancing a set distance each year.
Drylands cover about 41% of the earth's land surface and are home to about 2 billion people (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005).
The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994. 17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification.
notes.tip: Desertification is degradation of dryland, not the Sahara advancing a set distance each year.

notes.b: The Sahel is the semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan. Natural and human causes combine there, and some of the causes lie in other regions.
points: Rainfall is about 200–600 mm a year, falling in one short wet season, so crops and pasture are easily damaged by drought.
Physical causes: unreliable rainfall and drought, notably in the 1970s and 1980s.

Human causes: population growth, overgrazing, overcultivation and fuelwood collection. Cash crops (crops grown for sale) such as groundnuts in Senegal and cotton take the best land for export, and nomads have been settled, which concentrates grazing on smaller areas.
Global warming, linked to emissions in other regions, adds to drought.
Effects: famine, conflict over land and water, and migration to cities and to Europe. Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s; a widely quoted UN figure puts the shrinkage at about 90%.
The Great Green Wall (African Union, 2007) is a planned band about 8,000 km long from Senegal to Djibouti, aiming to restore 100 million hectares by 2030. Progress has been slow.
Zaï pits (small planting holes) and stone lines, used in Yatenga, Burkina Faso, by farmers such as Yacouba Sawadogo, trap water and soil.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration (farmers protecting trees that regrow on their land) in Niger has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s, in the Maradi and Zinder regions.
notes.tip: Show the interdependence: export cash crops and emissions elsewhere contribute, and the effects (migration to Europe) reach other regions.

notes.b: The Aral Sea shows how a decision made in one capital destroyed an environment and a fishing economy in other countries.
points: In 1960 the Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the world's fourth-largest lake.
From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton. The sea shrank to a small fraction of its size and split.
Fishing collapsed because the water shrank, and the port of Moynaq was left far from the shore.
Salt and pesticide dust storms now blow from the exposed seabed, because the sea no longer covers it.
The loss was caused by irrigation, not by climate change.
The Kok-Aral Dam (2005, Kazakhstan, with World Bank funding) raised the North Aral Sea, and fishing has partly recovered.
notes.tip: The Aral Sea shrank because of irrigation, not climate change.

notes.b: Dryland damage is not only an African problem. In Europe it is linked to what supermarkets sell, and in China to a huge tree-planting scheme.
points: Almería, in south-east Spain, is one of the driest parts of Europe. Tens of thousands of hectares of plastic greenhouses grow vegetables in winter for northern European supermarkets, including those in Ireland.
The greenhouses are irrigated largely from groundwater, which is being over-pumped, so the water supply of a dry region is being used up.
China's Three-North Shelter Forest Programme, begun in 1978 and due to run to 2050, plants belts of trees across northern China to hold back the Gobi and reduce dust storms.
Many trees have died where they were planted in unsuitable dry areas, so the scheme has had mixed results.

notes.b: Global warming is the rise in the planet's average temperature caused by greenhouse gases (gases that trap heat in the atmosphere). Emissions in some countries cause effects for everyone.
points: Greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels in industrialised and emerging economies, from deforestation and from agriculture cause global warming.
Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s (Mauna Loa).

Global average surface temperature, a key measure of warming, has risen about 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC). 2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus).
China has been the largest CO2 emitter since the mid-2000s, because of its industry, but the USA emits far more per person.
Rich countries bear historical responsibility for much of the emissions that have built up in the atmosphere, because they industrialised first.
notes.tip: Global warming is not the same as ozone depletion or acid rain. Keep them separate.

notes.h: Global warming: effects on other areas
notes.b: This is the clearest interdependence point. Countries that emitted least often suffer most, because they are low-lying, dry or poor.
points: Countries that emitted least suffer most, for example Bangladesh. Bangladesh, in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, faces floods, cyclones and sea-level rise.
Small island states, such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives, are threatened by sea-level rise.
Global sea level, which rises as ice melts and seawater warms, rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Arctic summer sea ice, which melts as the air warms, has shrunk by about 13% per decade since 1979.
The Great Barrier Reef has suffered repeated mass bleaching (corals losing their colour when stressed by warm water) since the late 1990s.

Pakistan's floods of 2022 followed extreme monsoon rains and glacier melt. About a third of the country was flooded, over 1,700 people died and about 33 million were affected. Pakistan produces under 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it caused very little of the warming that worsened the floods.
Drought in the Sahel, rising food prices when harvests fail, and climate-driven migration spread the effects across regions.
notes.tip: Name Pakistan and Bangladesh as examples of countries hit hard by warming they did little to cause.

notes.b: Ireland both contributes to warming and feels its effects.
points: Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions. Transport produces about a fifth (EPA, early 2020s).
Ireland's average temperature has risen about 0.9 °C since 1900.
Storm Éowyn, in January 2025, is an example of the more extreme weather that warming brings.
The Climate Act 2021 sets a 51% cut in emissions by 2030 (from 2018) and net zero (cutting emissions until what remains is balanced by removals) by 2050.

notes.b: No country can solve warming alone, so responses are agreements between countries. The key ones are listed by date, with an evaluation at the end.
points: The UNFCCC (the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change), agreed at Rio de Janeiro in 1992, set up the framework for international co-operation.

The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) was never ratified (formally approved) by the USA, so the largest economy was outside it. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C.

The EU Emissions Trading System (a market in permits to emit carbon) began in 2005. The European Green Deal (2019) aims for climate neutrality by 2050 and at least a 55% cut by 2030 compared with 1990.
COP30 (the annual UN climate conference) was held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.

The Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (2022) and became operational at COP28 in Dubai (2023), to help countries hit by climate damage, such as poor countries that emitted little.

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) required reporting from October 2023 for imports such as steel, cement, aluminium and fertilisers. Importers will pay for the carbon in these goods from 2026, so EU climate decisions affect exporters such as China and India.
Evaluation: national pledges still fall short of the 1.5 °C goal, so co-operation between countries is essential.
notes.tip: Include responses needing co-operation and finish with an evaluation: pledges still fall short of 1.5 °C.

notes.h: Refugees, asylum seekers and other migrants
notes.b: Different kinds of movers have different legal status, and examiners expect them to be kept apart.
points: An economic migrant moves voluntarily for work and a better life.

Under the UN Refugee Convention (1951), a refugee has a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Its 1967 Protocol removed the time and place limits.
An asylum seeker has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision.
An internally displaced person has been forced to flee but remains inside their own country, so, unlike a refugee, has not crossed a border.
A stateless person is not recognised as a national by any state, so no government is responsible for protecting them.
UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.

Political refugees flee persecution or war that results from political decisions. Economic 'refugees' flee poverty, often caused by decisions elsewhere in trade, debt or conflict. The line between them is often blurred.
notes.tip: Refugee, asylum seeker, economic migrant and internally displaced person are four different things. Ukrainians in the EU have temporary protection, not asylum.

notes.b: Displacement is large, but the burden falls mainly on countries close to the conflict rather than on Europe.
points: More than 120 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide in 2024 (UNHCR), including refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced people.
Most refugees stay in neighbouring countries, because they can reach them most easily, mostly low- and middle-income ones, not in Europe.
Turkey hosted the largest refugee population in the world for most of the 2010s and early 2020s, mostly Syrians.

notes.b: Syria is the main case of political refugees: a government's violent response to protest led to war and to a movement of people across several countries and into Europe. Each step is a decision in one place with effects in another.
points: Protests in March 2011 were met with force by President Bashar al-Assad's government, leading to civil war.
Syria's pre-war population was about 22 million. At the height of the war over half were displaced, including over 6 million refugees abroad and a similar number displaced inside Syria.
Turkey hosted over 3 million Syrian refugees. Lebanon has the most refugees per head of population of any country. Zaatari camp in Jordan opened in 2012, to house refugees arriving from Syria.
Alan Kurdi, a three-year-old Syrian boy, drowned and was photographed on a beach near Bodrum, Turkey, on 2 September 2015. The image changed public opinion in Europe.
About 1.3 million asylum applications were made in the EU in 2015.
Germany's decision to admit refugees, with Merkel's 'Wir schaffen das' (August 2015). Hungary built a border fence with Serbia in 2015, to block people crossing.
EU–Turkey statement (March 2016): irregular migrants were returned from the Greek islands to Turkey, and the EU was to provide €6 billion for refugees in Turkey.
The Assad government fell on 8 December 2024. Many refugees began to consider return, but homes, services and the economy were destroyed.
notes.tip: Syria figures are rounded and approximate. Do not give a death toll for the Syrian war.

notes.b: The Rohingya case shows what happens when a state refuses to recognise a people as citizens, so that no state protects them.
points: The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim minority from Rakhine State, Myanmar.
Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law did not recognise them as one of the country's national groups, leaving most of them stateless, which means no state owes them protection.
From August 2017 a military campaign of killings and village burning drove about 740,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh.
About 1 million Rohingya live in camps around Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, including Kutupalong, the world's largest refugee camp. Restrictions limit their work and movement, so they depend on aid.
From 2020 Bangladesh moved some refugees to Bhasan Char, a flood-prone island, which is a risk for the people moved there, in the Bay of Bengal.
A UN fact-finding mission (2018) called for Myanmar's generals to be investigated for genocide. The Gambia brought a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019.
The military coup in Myanmar in February 2021 ended prospects of a safe return.
notes.tip: Do not give a death toll for the Rohingya campaign, because estimates vary.

notes.b: Ukraine shows how a quick EU decision gave millions of people rights at once. It also raises a question about how other asylum seekers are treated.
points: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022. It is a political decision that displaced millions.
The EU Temporary Protection Directive (2001) was activated for the first time on 4 March 2022, giving immediate rights to live and work, so people did not have to wait for an asylum decision.
Temporary protection is not asylum. Over 4 million people held temporary protection in the EU in 2024, and Ireland had received over 100,000 Ukrainians by 2024.
UNHCR recorded over 6 million refugees from Ukraine across Europe (2023–24).
The contrast with the treatment of asylum seekers from Africa and the Middle East raises a question of equality in human rights.
notes.tip: Ukrainians in the EU have temporary protection, not asylum.

notes.b: Ireland's own system for refugees has changed over time and has met pressure on accommodation, which led to protests.
points: The Refugee Act 1996 and the International Protection Act 2015 set out Ireland's protection system. Direct provision (State-run accommodation for asylum seekers) was introduced in 2000.
Asylum seekers gained the right to work, after a waiting period, from 2018, following a 2017 Supreme Court ruling.
Over 13,000 international protection applications were made in 2022. A 2021 White Paper planned to end direct provision by 2024, but the plan was abandoned as numbers rose.
Accommodation is run by IPAS (the International Protection Accommodation Services).
Protests: East Wall from November 2022, and a riot in Dublin on 23 November 2023.
The Irish Refugee Protection Programme (September 2015) offered protection to up to 4,000 people, in response to the Syrian crisis.

notes.b: Migration is mostly between neighbouring countries, with a few large flows between regions.
points: About 281 million international migrants were counted in 2020 (IOM World Migration Report 2022), about 3.6% of the world's population.
Most international migrants move within their own region, for example within Africa, South–South as well as South–North.
Main corridors: Mexico–USA; North and West Africa–Europe; and South Asia–the Gulf.
Eastern–Western Europe migration followed EU enlargement on 1 May 2004, when new member states joined.

notes.h: Economic migration and the decisions behind it
notes.b: Economic migration is shaped by political decisions, such as opening a labour market, recruiting foreign workers or fishing policy. These examples show decisions in one place driving movement to another.
points: On 1 May 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing EU members to open their labour markets to the new members at once.
Migrant workers, mainly from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan and the Philippines, make up most of the population and workforce of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
The kafala system ties a migrant worker's legal status to an employer-sponsor.

Qatar was criticised over conditions for workers building World Cup stadiums and infrastructure. It introduced reforms in 2020, a minimum wage and the right to change jobs without the employer's permission, but enforcement has been criticised. The FIFA World Cup was held in Qatar in November–December 2022.
The Atlantic route: migrants from Senegal, Mauritania, Mali and elsewhere in West Africa travel by boat to Spain's Canary Islands. Arrivals reached a record in 2024.

Senegalese fishermen have blamed foreign industrial trawler fleets and fishmeal factories for declining catches, which they say pushes young men to migrate. This is a reported cause, not a proven one.
The Central Mediterranean route: the Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people. Italy's Mare Nostrum operation ran in 2013–14.
notes.tip: Economic migration questions look for the Gulf and remittances. Present the Senegalese fishing claim as a reported cause, not proven fact.

notes.h: Remittances and effects on source and receiving regions
notes.b: Migration changes both the country people leave (the source) and the country they go to (the receiving region).
points: Remittances (money sent home by migrants) to low- and middle-income countries were about $650 billion in 2023, more than foreign direct investment and official aid to those countries combined (excluding China) (World Bank).
India is the largest recipient of remittances and Mexico the second (2023).
Source regions: brain drain (the loss of skilled people) of doctors and nurses, loss of young workers, and return migrants who bring skills and capital.
Receiving regions: migrants fill jobs in health care, construction, farming and hospitality, and younger populations offset ageing, because many migrants are young workers.
Receiving regions: cultural diversity, but also pressure on housing and services and political reaction from anti-immigration parties.
The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted in May 2024 and applies from mid-2026. Ireland opted in.

notes.b: Ireland has been a country of mass emigration and is now a country of net immigration, shaped by political and economic decisions.
points: The Great Famine (1845–49): about 1 million died and about 1 million emigrated, in a system shaped by the land system and government policy.
Net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, and over 200,000 between 1981 and 1991.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013, after the crash of 2008.
Census 2022: about 12% of residents were non-Irish nationals, and just over 1 million people were born outside Ireland. Ireland has returned to net immigration (more people arriving than leaving).
notes.tip: Expect a question on Ireland's experience as part of refugees, migration patterns and human rights.

notes.b: Human rights are set out in international agreements. Governments' decisions can protect these rights or violate them.
points: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948), Article 14, gives the right to seek and enjoy asylum from persecution.
Non-refoulement, the principle that refugees must not be returned to danger, is set out in Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention.
The European Convention on Human Rights, of the Council of Europe, was signed in 1950.
Political decisions can protect these rights or violate them.

notes.h: Human rights in global supply chains
notes.b: A supply chain is the series of firms that make a product. When rich-country brands and consumers choose where to buy, they affect the rights of workers in poor countries.
points: Rana Plaza, Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing about 1,130 people and injuring about 2,500. Its factories supplied Western brands, including Primark, founded in Dublin in 1969 as Penneys.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was signed in May 2013 in response, so the disaster led to a safety agreement.

Xinjiang, China: the UN Human Rights Office (2022) reported serious violations against Uyghurs and other mainly Muslim groups, including mass detention. There is evidence of forced labour in cotton and other industries.
Xinjiang grows most of China's cotton, about a fifth of the world's cotton, so forced labour there can enter many clothing chains.

The US Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (signed December 2021, in force June 2022) presumes that goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang use forced labour and bans their import unless proven otherwise.
ILO and UNICEF estimated about 160 million children in child labour in 2020, about 70% of them in agriculture.
Child labour in cobalt mining (the DR Congo mines in the Apple case) and the treatment of migrant workers in Qatar show the same pattern: rich-country decisions affect workers in poor ones.
notes.tip: Cover human rights through the UDHR, supply chains and the treatment of refugees.

notes.h: Decisions in one country affecting human rights in another
notes.b: Individuals, governments and the EU can act to protect rights abroad. The Irish anti-apartheid strike is the main Irish example.
points: In July 1984 Mary Manning, a worker at Dunnes Stores, Henry Street, Dublin, refused to handle South African grapefruit in protest against apartheid (South Africa's system of racial segregation). She was suspended, and a small group of colleagues went on strike with her for almost three years.
In 1987, because of the protest, the Irish government banned imports of South African fruit and vegetables.
Apartheid in South Africa lasted from 1948 to 1994, so the Dunnes strike took place in its later decades.
Sanctions (penalties such as limits on trade) were applied to apartheid South Africa and, later, to Myanmar and Russia. A decision in one country restricts trade and investment with another.
The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, adopted in 2024, requires large companies to address human rights risks in their supply chains.

notes.h: Human rights and the treatment of refugees
notes.b: Refugees' rights are often at risk on the journey and after arrival, as these examples from the earlier cases show.
points: Examples include detention, pushbacks (forcing people back across a border) and deaths at sea in the Mediterranean, including the Lampedusa shipwreck above.
Long stays in direct provision in Ireland, for example, raise questions of dignity and human rights.
Children's education in camps and women's safety in camps are human rights concerns.
Statelessness, as with the Rohingya, leaves people without the protection of any state.

notes.b: To finish an essay on social and political decisions, step back and judge what the cases show.
points: Decisions about war, borders, trade and aid in one country shape the lives of people far away. The Syria, Rohingya and Ukraine cases show this.
Effective responses need international co-operation through bodies such as UNHCR, the EU and the UN Refugee Convention.
notes.tip: Use this to close an answer: decisions in one country shape lives far away, and effective responses need international co-operation.

keyTerms.definition: The reliance of countries and regions on each other, so that a decision in one place has effects elsewhere.
A region that supplies raw materials, components or assembly for products sold elsewhere.
A region that buys finished products, mostly rich countries and increasingly China and India.
A $400 a tonne addition to cocoa sales from the 2020–21 season, intended to raise farmers' incomes in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.
The clearing of forest for farming, mining, roads and other uses, with effects on climate, biodiversity and people.
Land degradation in drylands caused by climate and by human activity such as overgrazing, overcultivation and irrigation.
The semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, where drought and land degradation have caused famine and migration.
Harvesting timber no faster than the forest grows, so that the stock is maintained.
Cutting down all the trees in an area at once, usually followed by replanting.
The rise in average surface temperature caused mainly by greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture.
An EU scheme under which importers of certain goods pay for the carbon emitted in producing them.
A person who moves voluntarily to another country to work or to seek a better life.
A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution and is outside their country, as defined by the 1951 Refugee Convention.
A person who has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision.
A person forced to flee their home who remains inside their own country.
A person not recognised as a national by any state.
The principle that refugees must not be returned to a country where they face danger.
A legal status giving displaced people immediate rights to live and work in the EU, without the asylum process.
A sponsorship system that ties a migrant worker's legal status to an employer in some Gulf states.
Money sent home by migrants to family in their countries of origin.
The Irish system of housing asylum seekers in state-run accommodation while their applications are processed.

factCards.term: Apple's iPhone chain: where each stage takes place
factCards.definition: Designed in Cupertino, California; chips from TSMC (Taiwan); screens from Samsung and LG (South Korea); cobalt mostly from the DR Congo; assembly mainly by Taiwanese Foxconn at Zhengzhou and Shenzhen, China, and by Foxconn and Tata in India.

factCards.term: Apple: who gains most, and how consumer regions are affected
factCards.definition: A 2011 study (Kraemer, Linden, Dedrick) estimated Apple kept about 58% of the 2010 iPhone's price as profit, Chinese assembly labour under 2%. Profits and design and marketing jobs stay in the USA; consumers get new technology; e-waste goes to poorer countries.

factCards.term: Apple: three benefits for producer regions
factCards.definition: Assembly and supplier firms employ millions of people; China gains skills, industrial growth and export earnings; supplier firms such as TSMC and Foxconn grow on the strength of Apple's orders.

factCards.term: Apple: four problems for producer regions
factCards.definition: Foxconn worker suicides in Shenzhen (2010) exposed long hours and pressure; Zhengzhou workers protested over pay and lockdown (November 2022), delaying iPhones worldwide; orders can move to India; child labour in the DR Congo's cobalt mines (Amnesty, 2016).

factCards.term: Apple in Cork: when it came and what it does there
factCards.definition: Apple, founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980, its first manufacturing plant in Europe. About 6,000 now work there in its European headquarters and support centre; Cork does not assemble iPhones.

factCards.term: Apple: two decisions elsewhere that affected Ireland and Apple
factCards.definition: In 2016 the European Commission ruled Ireland gave Apple €13 billion in illegal State aid (not a fine); overturned in 2020, it was reinstated in September 2024, so Ireland got about €14 billion. US tariffs (2018, 2025) pushed Apple to assemble more in India.

factCards.term: Cadbury and Mondelēz: ownership history and Irish plants
factCards.definition: Founded by John Cadbury in Birmingham in 1824; bought by Kraft Foods in 2010; part of Mondelēz International, Chicago, since 2012. Irish plants: Coolock, Dublin (chocolate) and Rathmore, Co. Kerry (crumb from local milk for factories in Britain).

factCards.term: Cocoa producer regions: where cocoa grows and who adds the value
factCards.definition: Côte d'Ivoire grows about two-fifths of world cocoa and Ghana is second: together over half, mostly on small family farms, exported as beans. The value is added mostly outside Africa: the Netherlands (Amsterdam) is the world's largest cocoa-processing centre.

factCards.term: Cocoa: child labour and deforestation in producer regions
factCards.definition: A 2020 NORC study for the US Department of Labor found about 1.56 million children in cocoa child labour in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana; Harkin–Engel Protocol (2001) deadlines were missed. Côte d'Ivoire has lost most of its forest since 1960, much to cocoa.

factCards.term: Cocoa's record price in 2024: why farmers gained little
factCards.definition: Poor West African harvests, from bad weather and the cocoa swollen shoot virus, pushed prices to a record above $10,000 a tonne. Farmers in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana gained far less, because their governments fix farm-gate prices in advance.

factCards.term: Cadbury's responses to cocoa problems, and the criticism
factCards.definition: Cadbury Dairy Milk carried the Fairtrade Mark from 2009. Mondelēz began its own Cocoa Life programme in 2012 (about $400 million over ten years); in 2017 Dairy Milk in Britain and Ireland swapped Fairtrade for the Cocoa Life logo, criticised by campaigners.

factCards.term: Chocolate: consumer regions and how they pressure producers
factCards.definition: Europe and North America eat most chocolate; brands, marketing and retail take most of the price. The EU Deforestation Regulation (2023, delayed) will make firms prove cocoa, soya, palm oil and similar goods were not grown on land deforested after 2020.

factCards.term: Managed forests in Sweden and Finland: how they stay sustainable
factCards.definition: Forest covers about two-thirds of Sweden and three-quarters of Finland. Sweden's 1903 Forestry Act made owners replant; the 1993 Act balanced timber and nature. Growth exceeds felling, so standing volume has doubled since the 1920s. Buyers demand FSC or PEFC.

factCards.term: Scandinavian forestry: exports and criticisms
factCards.definition: Sweden and Finland are among the leading exporters of pulp, paper and sawn timber (UPM, Stora Enso); Swedish IKEA is a major wood buyer. Critics: clear-felling and replanting with Norway spruce and Scots pine creates monocultures, removes old-growth forest and destroys lichen Sámi reindeer graze.

factCards.term: Pakistan floods 2022: global warming's unequal impact
factCards.definition: Extreme monsoon rains and glacier melt flooded about a third of the country; over 1,700 people died and about 33 million were affected. Pakistan produces under 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it suffers from emissions made elsewhere.

factCards.term: The Rohingya: how political decisions made them stateless refugees
factCards.definition: Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left most stateless; a 2017 army campaign drove about 740,000 into Bangladesh, where about 1 million live around Cox's Bazar. The Gambia sued Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (2019); the 2021 coup ended return hopes.

factCards.term: Ukraine 2022: the EU decision on temporary protection
factCards.definition: After Russia invaded (24 February 2022) the EU activated its Temporary Protection Directive for the first time, on 4 March 2022. Over 4 million held it in the EU and over 100,000 came to Ireland (2024). Asylum seekers from Africa and the Middle East get no such status: an equality question.

factCards.term: Global migration: scale and four main corridors
factCards.definition: About 281 million international migrants in 2020, 3.6% of the world's people, most within their own region. Corridors: Mexico–USA; North and West Africa–Europe; South Asia–the Gulf; East to West Europe after 2004, when Ireland opened its labour market at once.

factCards.term: Gulf migration: who goes, the kafala system and Qatar's reforms
factCards.definition: Migrants, mainly from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan and the Philippines, make up most of the people of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates; kafala ties them to an employer. Qatar's 2020 reforms (minimum wage, job mobility) followed World Cup criticism, but enforcement is criticised.

factCards.term: Atlantic and Mediterranean migration routes: key facts
factCards.definition: Migrants from Senegal, Mauritania and Mali sail to the Canary Islands, with record arrivals in 2024; Senegalese fishermen blame foreign trawlers and fishmeal plants for falling catches (a reported cause). Over 360 drowned off Lampedusa in October 2013.

factCards.term: Migration: effects on source and receiving regions
factCards.definition: Source: about $650 billion in remittances to low- and middle-income countries (2023), India the largest recipient and Mexico second; brain drain of doctors and nurses. Receiving: workers for health care, building and farming; younger populations; housing pressure; anti-immigration parties.

factCards.term: Xinjiang: forced labour and the US import ban
factCards.definition: UN Human Rights Office (2022): serious violations against Uyghurs, including mass detention. There is also evidence of forced labour in cotton; Xinjiang grows about a fifth of world cotton. The US Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (in force June 2022) bans Xinjiang goods unless proven clean.

factCards.term: Dunnes Stores strike: one worker's decision and its effect
factCards.definition: In July 1984 Mary Manning, at Dunnes Stores, Henry Street, Dublin, refused to handle South African grapefruit in protest at apartheid; she and a few colleagues struck for almost three years. In 1987 Ireland banned South African fruit and vegetable imports.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of global trading patterns on both producer and consumer regions, with reference to one multinational company that you have studied.
questions.model: Apple is a US company headquartered in Cupertino, California, which designs its products there and outsources manufacturing. Its iPhone, launched in 2007, is assembled mostly in China by Foxconn, a Taiwanese contract manufacturer, at Zhengzhou and Shenzhen, and increasingly in India, by Foxconn and the Indian Tata group near Chennai and Bengaluru. Producer regions gain jobs, skills, export earnings and supplier growth: TSMC in Taiwan makes Apple's chips, and Samsung and LG in South Korea supply screens. The negative impacts are considerable. A 2011 study by Kraemer, Linden and Dedrick estimated that Apple kept about 58% of the sale price of an iPhone as profit, while Chinese assembly labour received under 2%. Worker suicides at Foxconn's Shenzhen factories in 2010 drew attention to long hours and pressure, and the Zhengzhou protest of November 2022 delayed iPhone supplies worldwide. Producer regions depend on orders that can move, and assembly has shifted towards India after US tariffs from 2018 and 2025. Cobalt from the DR Congo is mined in conditions that Amnesty International (2016) documented, including child labour. Consumer regions in Europe and North America gain access to new technology and services and pay high prices, while most profit and high-paid design and marketing jobs stay in the USA. Electronic waste is exported to poorer countries. Ireland's position is distinctive. Apple's Cork campus, opened in 1980 as its first European plant, employs about 6,000 people and is its European headquarters, though it does not assemble iPhones. The EU state-aid case, in which the Commission ruled in 2016 that Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth €13 billion, was reinstated by the EU Court of Justice in September 2024, and Ireland received about €14 billion including interest. A decision in Brussels therefore affected both Ireland and the USA. Evaluation: the chain transfers jobs and growth to producer regions but concentrates value, power and profit in the company's home base and in the consumer regions that buy its products.

questions.prompt: We live in an interdependent global economy where decisions taken in one area have an impact on other areas. Examine this statement with reference to deforestation, global warming and desertification.
questions.model: Deforestation shows interdependence through demand. The Amazon, the world's largest tropical rainforest, lost close to a fifth of its original forest, with cattle ranching the largest cause and soya spreading north from Mato Grosso, much of it exported as animal feed to Europe and China. PRODES figures show about 27,800 km² cleared in 2004, about 4,600 km² in 2012 and about 13,000 km² in 2021, before a sharp fall from 2023. The effects reach beyond Brazil: released carbon adds to global warming, and reduced rainfall recycling affects farming elsewhere. Responses involve other countries, including the Amazon Soy Moratorium of 2006 and the Amazon Fund of 2008, which Norway funds most. In contrast, the managed forests of Sweden and Finland show a sustainable alternative: Sweden's 1903 Forestry Act required replanting, its standing timber has roughly doubled since the 1920s, and certification by the FSC, founded in 1993, is demanded by buyers in other countries. Critics of clear-felling argue that it creates monocultures and removes old-growth forest, and it destroys the lichen on which Sámi herders' reindeer graze in winter. Global warming is the clearest case of interdependence. Rich countries and China, the largest CO2 emitter since the mid-2000s, cause most of the emissions, while Bangladesh, the Maldives, Tuvalu and Kiribati face sea-level rise and Pakistan's 2022 floods, which affected about 33 million people, followed extreme rain and glacier melt, although Pakistan produces under 1% of global emissions. Responses require co-operation through the UNFCCC of 1992, the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement of 2015, the Loss and Damage Fund and the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which charges importers for the carbon in their goods from 2026. Desertification in the Sahel shows the same chain. Drought, overgrazing, overcultivation and cash crops such as groundnuts and cotton grown for export degrade the land, and famine, conflict and migration follow, while the shrinking of Lake Chad reflects regional pressures. The Great Green Wall and zaï pits are local responses, but progress is slow. The Aral Sea shows that decisions by Soviet planners to divert rivers for cotton destroyed a sea and its fishing economy in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, with salt and dust storms spreading far beyond it. Evaluation: decisions about trade, energy and consumption in one place cause degradation elsewhere, so the statement is well supported, though responses remain limited.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of social and political decisions with reference to economic and political refugees, migration patterns and human rights issues.
questions.model: Political decisions create political refugees. Syria's government met protests in March 2011 with force, leading to civil war; over half the population was displaced, including over 6 million refugees abroad, with Turkey hosting over 3 million, Lebanon having the most refugees per head of any country, and Zaatari camp in Jordan opened in 2012. The 2015 movement to Europe, with about 1.3 million asylum applications in the EU that year, followed Alan Kurdi's photograph of 2 September 2015 and German and Hungarian decisions, and the EU–Turkey statement of March 2016 returned irregular migrants from the Greek islands to Turkey in exchange for €6 billion. The Rohingya show statelessness: Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left them without recognition, and the 2017 military campaign drove about 740,000 into Bangladesh, where about 1 million live in camps around Cox's Bazar, including Kutupalong. The Gambia's 2019 genocide case at the International Court of Justice and the 2021 coup have left return uncertain. Economic migration is driven by decisions too. About 281 million people were international migrants in 2020, most moving within their own region, and migrant workers from South Asia and the Philippines make up most of the workforce of Qatar and the UAE under the kafala system, with Qatar's 2020 reforms criticised for enforcement. Migrants from West Africa take the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, with record arrivals in 2024, and the Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people. Remittances of about $650 billion to low- and middle-income countries in 2023 support families, though source regions also lose doctors and young workers. Ireland's experience includes the Great Famine of 1845–49 and emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, and its refugee system, with direct provision since 2000 and the right to work from 2018. Human rights frameworks protect these people: Article 14 of the UDHR of 1948 gives the right to seek asylum, and non-refoulement is set out in Article 33 of the 1951 Convention. Human rights issues also arise in supply chains: the Rana Plaza collapse of 2013 killed about 1,130 people, and the US ban on goods made with forced labour in Xinjiang responds to the UN's 2022 report. Decisions also cross borders in the other direction: in 1984 Mary Manning, a worker at Dunnes Stores in Dublin, refused to handle South African grapefruit, and the Irish government banned South African fruit and vegetables in 1987. Evaluation: decisions on war, borders, trade and aid shape the lives of people far away, so effective responses need international co-operation through UNHCR, the EU and the UN Refugee Convention.
